s: Sourcing finished, purchasing frozen Our first plan was a sealed growth chamber with hydroponics inside it. Arabidopsis needs steady humidity, temperature and light to give comparable results, and the school lab could not hold any of those steady. The chamber was meant to give us a controlled box to run every plant experiment in. This was the last week of design before we started buying parts. GROWTH CHAMBER · PRE-PIVOT · WEEK pre Timmy, Noah, Anton, Chloe Finished the chamber layout and ran airflow studies on the enclosure. Fans, ducting and shelf spacing sized around a how many trays? tray capacity. Built four sourcing lists, split by where we would actually buy each part. Electronics and control from Guanghua. Structure from Test Rite. Plants and water systems from the Jianguo flower market. Containers from IKEA. Fans, timers, DS18B20 temperature sensors, blackout cloth, a Mylar substitute, air pumps and air stones. Total came to NT$ ? . Stopped on 28 March, told to buy nothing and print nothing. The instructors were still weighing the effort against the risk and against what the chamber would be worth to us later. Nothing had been ordered, so the freeze cost us planning time and nothing else. Freeze purchasing instead of building in parallel If half of it was already built we’d have argued to keep going. We hadn’t spent anything yet, so stopping was free. Ordering the slow-

Visiting Prof. Verslues We had a chamber design nobody had agreed to and a purchasing freeze. None of us had seen a working plant growth setup, so we went to look at one before designing any more of our own. HUMIDITY BOX · ORIGIN · WEEK pre Anton, Noah Visited Prof. Verslues at institution on 3 April. He works on his research area . Looked at how his incubator holds conditions across a whole tray at once. Trays sit on wire shelving with airflow coming from underneath. He grows at a much lower density than we had been planning for. Came back and dropped the full chamber in favour of a humidity box. Humidity is the condition that decides whether the seeds come up, and a box holding one tray is a build we could actually finish. Build a humidity box, not a growth chamber Small enough that we’d actually finish it. Humidity is the condition that decides whether the seeds come up. Carrying on with the full chamber. It was frozen anyway, and after seeing a real one we couldn’t justify the size. No target humidity range written down, and nothing to measure it with Get the range Arabidopsis needs, and put a sensor on the next electronics order. Design the box around a target humidity range, not around the space we happen to have.

Told to drop soil sensing Our original plan was to sense drought stress in soil and release protectant into the soil directly. Before committing to it we wanted someone who sells into agriculture to tell us whether it held up. DIRECTION · PROF. CHEN · CONSULTATION pre Anton, Timmy, Jessie Had an online meeting with Prof. Chen of institution , who works on field , on 10 April. He has commercial products in the smart agriculture market we were aiming at. Were told to drop soil moisture sensing entirely. Cheap sensors already dominate that market and they are inaccurate. Calibrating a sensor across soil types takes three to four months of data for each one. Took his second point, that soil release is hard to defend on biosafety. Engineered bacteria going into open soil is a much harder case to make than bacteria kept inside a vessel. He pushed us toward containment. Reframed the business model around the consumable rather than the device. Sell the cartridge, not the box, the way printers and ink work. His idea, not ours. Drop soil sensing and move to a contained vessel A market already served by cheap sensors is not one we can enter with a school budget. Containment is easier to defend than release, and we were going to be asked about it. Soil calibration across types. Three to four months of data for each one, which we do not have. t: The pivot, and asking Dr. Pak where to start
s: The pivot, and asking Dr. Pak where to start This is the week the project changed shape. The pivot document went up on 15 April: instead of sensing soil and releasing into it, engineered B. subtilis would live inside a sealed vessel, and light would tell them when to produce protectant. That vessel is a bioreactor, and none of us had built one or knew where to start. BIOREACTOR · CONCEPT · CONSULTATION concept Anton, Noah, Timmy Posted the pivot on 15 April. Input soil stress, output green or red light into a contained chamber. Seven people reacted to the message. Every instrument in this notebook follows from it. Asked Dr. Pak, Dean of Research, for the reactor landscape. He set out five families. Continuous stirred tank, bubble column, air lift, fluidised bed, packed bed. He suggested a packed bed for our case, with bacteria immobilised in the column. He said bioreactor design is an enormous field and there is no need to invent something new. Adapting a common design to our needs would itself be the achievement. We went on to choose hollow-fibre tangential flow, which is not what he suggested. That conversation happened in person and nobody wrote down why. what else happened this week? Adapt an existing reactor design rather than invent one Adapting an existing design became the goal, so the scope stopped growing. Five families to choose from instead of a blank page. Nothing

Dropping the fluorometer The chlorophyll fluorometer would have let us measure plant stress directly, by reading damage to photosystem II. Fv/Fm is the standard number for that, and a healthy plant sits around 0.78 to 0.83. It was the fourth instrument we had in progress and there were three of us. FLUOROMETER · PHOTOMETER · WEEK FL / PH Timmy, Anton, Eva Made the case for building it. It measures the outcome the project claims to improve, so it would test our own claim directly. Anton moved to the bioreactor. Eva took a different task. The Open-JIP evaluation was never written up, so anyone picking it up starts from nothing. Wrote the photometer requirement on 16 May, in nine words. We need to measure flow rate, and how much B. subtilis there is. The shape of the answer followed immediately: flow cuvette plus spectrometer, 600 nm beam, a sensor reading light decay, an intensity controller. Drop the fluorometer on capacity, not feasibility The science holds up. It was never a feasibility problem, only a staffing one. Better to finish two instruments than half-finish three. t: Building the agar plate imaging station
s: Building the agar plate imaging station The imaging station is a rig that holds a phone in a fixed position over an agar plate, under fixed lighting, so photos taken days apart can be compared. It is the answer to the problem from last week. IMAGING STATION · BUILD IS-1 Anton, Noah Built a four-legged frame with a slot at the top for the phone. Bending an LED strip into an angled circle makes it twist and compress along its length at once, and it buckles somewhere unpredictable. Putting ridges around the ring fixed it. A dead LED can be replaced without reprinting the ring, which takes six hours. Made the white bottom plate removable from underneath on four screws. Swap it for black and the photo background changes with no reprint. Every part of the station comes apart the same way. Bioreactor prototype I built The bioreactor is the vessel the pivot committed us to. Bacteria live inside a hollow fibre membrane while the protectant they make crosses the membrane and leaves, which keeps the organism contained. Prototype I is the simplest version of that we could build. BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE I · BUILD BR-1 Anton, Noah, Joshua, Chars Built prototype I on 6 June from four parts. Drove both light plate wavelengths for the first time, green 520 nm and red 660 nm. First row of wells only, driven independently. Green is the on command for the CcaS-CcaR circuit and red is the off command. Built the round vertical agar stand. what is it for, and how does it differ from the square one? t: The cells barely grow in the reactor
s: The cells barely grow in the reactor This is the first run of prototype I. We grew the same culture in the reactor and in a flask at the same time, both at room temperature, so the flask acts as a control. If the reactor works, the two curves should look alike. BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE I · FAILURE DIAGNOSIS BR-1 Gabriel, abby, Anton, Noah Sampled both arms every thirty minutes for eight hours, then again at 25 hours. One person had to stay with it for the whole run. Got a flask that climbed past 2.4 and a reactor that stayed almost flat near 0.3. The numbers inside the system disagreed too, 0.304 in the tube against 0.48 in the reservoir. That should not happen if the loop is mixed. Terminated early when medium leaked at the peristaltic pump. The leak was at the pump head, where the tubing flexes most. That is our evidence the membrane holds the bacteria in. It came out of the run that otherwise failed. Ruled out means we ran the test. To test means we have not. Change three things at once and accept we will not know which worked Stirring, temperature and sampling position are all cheap to change and all plausible. We have weeks, not months. We couldn’t afford to change one thing at a time. Testing one variable at a time. That’s the right way to do it and we chose speed instead. Writing it down here so nobody reads prototype II as proof that stirring alone fixed it. shell-side pl

t: Prototype II reaches plateau in two hours
s: Prototype II reaches plateau in two hours Prototype I barely grew and we had four candidate reasons. Prototype II changes three of them at once, which is not how you isolate a cause, but we had weeks rather than months. BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE II · TEST BR-2 Gabriel, abby, Anton, Noah Added a 200 rpm magnetic stirrer to the reservoir to stop cells settling out. The stirrer bar was the largest one we had, which may be part of why it worked so well. Moved the sampling port to the reservoir outlet, where there is far more volume. A sample from there represents the whole system rather than one length of tube. Ran both arms at 37 °C instead of room temperature, pump held at 94 mL/min. Got a full growth curve, and the reactor beat its own flask control. Reactor plateaued at OD600 0.8 to 0.9 after two hours. Flask reached 0.6 to 0.8 after four and a half. TABLE 11 Full growth curve secured. The reactor reached plateau faster and higher than the flask. Passed. Faster to plateau and higher than the control Faster to plateau and higher at plateau than the control, which is more than we expected. Whether stirring alone would have done it, we cannot say. Claiming stirring fixed it. Three variables moved and only one of them is in the headline. t: Prof. Chang finds the gap in the design
s: Prof. Chang finds the gap in the design Prof. Chang is a chair professor in chemical engineering at NCKU who has published on B. subtilis bioreactor systems, so he was the right person to show the design to. There was no valve on any plan before we spoke to him. Foaming from B. subtilis surfactant, which he mentioned twice. Resting cells. The cartridge format. Add a valve after the membrane A valve after the membrane is the mechanism we were missing entirely. Hydroponics as the delivery target, which also narrows the biosafety case. t: Wrong unit for the light dose
s: Wrong unit for the light dose The CcaS-CcaR circuit responds to a specific photon flux, so the light dose the plate delivers has to be a known quantity. This week we found we had been about to measure it in entirely the wrong unit. LIGHT PLATE · DOSE UNITS · TEST units Anton, Noah, Timmy Checked the Castillo-Hair paper and found its half-maximal point is 4.66 µmol per square metre per second. That is a photon flux density. It counts photons. Checked what our meters read, and found every affordable one reads illuminance in lux. Lux is weighted for human vision, which peaks around 555 nm. Our green sits at 520 and our red at 660, both well off that peak. So the conversion error is not even the same size on the two channels. Bought a lux meter and set out to derive the conversion for our own LED spectra. A proper PPFD sensor was out of budget. A phone app was considered and rejected as not repeatable between handsets. Caught it before any dose figure went out, so nothing published needs correcting. The factor we actually used is what factor did you use, and where from? and is not written down anywhere. Table 12a. The two units measure different things and cannot be converted without knowing the spectrum. Buy a lux meter and derive the conversion ourselves A proper PPFD sensor was out of budget and we needed a number that week. Quoting the paper’s number in lux and hoping. Every do

t: Temperature sensor driving the green channel
s: Temperature sensor driving the green channel The whole project is one sentence: sense stress, emit light, release protectant. This is the first time the sensing end and the light end ran together on a bench, two months after the pivot. STRESS TO LIGHT · FIRMWARE · BUILD demo Anton, Noah, Neo Wired an SHT31 temperature and humidity sensor to the Arduino over I2C. It reports humidity too, which the code reads and then ignores. Wrote a linear stress fraction between a floor and a ceiling temperature. Below 32 °C the LED is off. At 50 °C and above it is at full brightness. Between those it scales linearly. Mapped the fraction onto a PWM green channel and ran it. The transfer function is four lines of code, deliberately. Anything more shaped would be invented, since we have no data on how stress response scales with temperature. Wrote it up as Stress_to_Light_Demo_Manual.docx. 32 °C and 50 °C are guesses, not measurements. Only the green channel is driven, so the demo switches the circuit on but not off. Table 12b. Four constants and a straight line between two of them. Linear between two thresholds, nothing more shaped Two thresholds are easy to change once the wet lab gives us real numbers. Anything more shaped would be a guess dressed up as a model. A sigmoid or a lookup table. Neither is supported by anything we measured. serial output, stress fraction LED at full duty TEMP_BASE

Making the plate float Arabidopsis grows hydroponically on a plate sitting over liquid medium. The roots have to reach the liquid without the plate flooding, and our first version was fixed in place, which meant setting the level by hand every day and getting it wrong. HYDROPONICS · FLOATING PLATE · BUILD FP-1 Anton Built a fixed plate with a liquid chamber underneath, and found the level impossible to hold. It has to sit as high as possible without coming over the growing platform, and it drops as the plants drink, so the roots end up in air. Redesigned it to float on the medium instead. The frame of the platform is built as sealed air chambers, so it rides on the surface and stays at the same height above the liquid whatever the level does. Calculated the buoyancy before printing rather than tuning it afterwards. A hollow frame cannot be adjusted once printed, so print orientation and wall thickness now decide whether it floats. Added poles at the corners to take washers as weights. Adding weight is easier than adding volume, so the poles are the margin for error. The washers we have are heavier than the calculation wanted, so the adjustment is coarse. corner poles and washers floating in medium Printed the first iteration on 25 June. later iterations shrank it and added clip-in handles. when? t: Reading four times high on the reactor
s: Reading four times high on the reactor Iteration 4 is the final photometer build, with the component positions fixed, TPU-lined mounts so the glass is not scratched, and snap-in covers along the light path to block room light. This is the first time it went onto the reactor and got read against a benchtop instrument on the same culture. PHOTOMETER · ON THE REACTOR · TEST PH-4 Chars, Joshua, Noah, Anton Fitted it in line on the TFF loop and took a reading against the benchtop BioDrop. s: The photometer catches the pump failing The run had been going since 21 July and the curve was not the shape any of us expected. We spent most of the week arguing about why, then on 1 August it dropped and stayed down. PHOTOMETER · PUMP FAILURE · FAILURE DIAGNOSIS run Timmy, Noah, Joshua, Chars A healthy culture does not do that. We still cannot explain the shape. Guessed contamination when it dropped, that we were watching a second organism take over. That was wrong. We have left it in the record. Found the recirculation pump had failed. Chars confirmed on inspection and replaced it the same evening. Nobody was rostered to check the trace daily, which is why the drop was noticed late. Did not run the flush and reblank that would have separated fouling from biology. Once the run was torn down the chance was gone. Our first hypothesis was contamination. It was the pump. Chars confirmed on inspection and replaced it the same evening. Replace the pump and leave the trace intact The photometer caught a failure in the reactor with nobody watching, which is what we built it to be able to do. BIOREACTOR · PINCH VALVE · DECISION valve Chars, Noah, Anton, jacquelyn Wrote the criteria first so they could not be bent toward the answer we wanted. Whether it holds when power is cut. Holding force against the permeate pressure. Whether we can build it from parts already in the lab. How much firmware it needs. Scored a stepper, a servo and a solenoid out of five on each. The solenoid is unscored rather than zero. We could not source one in time. Chose the servo on the first criterion alone. A stepper lets go when it loses power and the loop is full of live culture. A servo stays tight. Holding on power loss is a safety property, so it outranks the other three. The servo we used is a spare from the VEX kit, not a part chosen for this. s: Where the bioreactor stands on 13 August This is the last week the notebook covers, not the last week of work. The bioreactor is part way through a rebuild and three problems are open, all of them mechanical. We had expected the biology to be the hard part. BIOREACTOR · NEXT PHASE · WEEK ongoing Anton, Noah, Joshua, Chars Started moving from the peristaltic pump to a magnetic one. A magnetic pump can be driven from the Arduino, which is what lets the system run without someone standing over it. It is weaker and cannot lift liquid out of the serum bottle. Planned a PC-cooler-style clear rectangle with ports top and bottom to get round the head problem. Feed in at the top, draw from the bottom, so gravity does some of the work. It was bought for its shape, not because it is designed for this. Found the dissolved oxygen and pH probes do not fit the reservoir cap. The cap has to be bored out. Keeping it airtight is the harder part, because the sensor body is thicker than its cable and the plug thicker again. Designed a cap in two halves that clamps around the cable and screws shut. Airtight, and nothing gets cut. The first approach was cutting each cable, threading it, and soldering it back. Sketched a sealed cartridge for replenishing B. subtilis, on the printer ink model.
